name: Surgery-first orthognathic approach
lead: The surgery-first orthognathic approach (SFOA) is a way of sequencing corrective jaw surgery in which the bone operation is done before, or without, the traditional period of pre-surgical orthodontic treatment with braces. Conventional orthognathic care uses braces before and after surgery, with the pre-surgical phase traditionally lasting up to about a year.[11]

Surgeons who use the approach cite advances in 3D virtual planning and in the use of miniscrews for orthodontic control after surgery, which they say allow stable occlusion without pre-surgical tooth decompensation.[1][2] Studies, mostly in skeletal class III patients from East Asia and Europe, have compared SFOA with the conventional sequence on treatment time, stability, quality of life and accuracy.[2][3][8]

The evidence base is mainly cohort and comparative studies; the sources reviewed describe a mix of findings, including reductions in total treatment time in some series and cautions about precautions and complications.[2][10] Within looksmaxxing culture it is discussed as the route by which people hoping for a faster change in facial structure pursue jaw surgery.

paras: Orthognathic surgery reshapes the jaws to treat bite, growth, airway and appearance problems and is usually done through the mouth. Traditionally, braces are worn before surgery to align the teeth over the jaws, and again afterwards to finish the bite.[11] Surgery-first and clear-aligner approaches are described as newer variations.[11]

A 2015 report from one surgical group describes adopting surgery-first without pre-surgical orthodontics for skeletal class III deformity, pointing to advances in pre-surgical orthodontic simulation and post-surgical miniscrew-assisted treatment.[1] A 2017 prospective study framed the question as whether the approach can reduce total treatment time.[2]
Proponents of the approach also describe an earlier improvement in facial appearance, since the jaw is corrected at the start rather than after months of braces.[3][4]

Because teeth are not pre-aligned, the planned surgical occlusion setup is central. Published work has described guidelines and accuracy of occlusal setups in class III correction,[9] and compared 3D planning with actual outcomes in surgery-first cases.[7]
A comparative study of postoperative stability after bilateral sagittal split ramus osteotomy for class III correction examined conventional surgery against surgery-first.[8]

A 2019 review, the second part of a series on the current status of the approach, discusses precautions and complications specific to surgery-first.[10] General orthognathic risks include bleeding, swelling, infection, and nerve injury with facial numbness that usually recovers within months but is rarely permanent.[11]

A 2017 prospective study investigated whether surgery-first reduces total treatment time compared with conventional treatment.[2] Two questionnaire-based studies compared oral health-related quality of life and satisfaction: one with 15 patients per arm[3] and one longitudinal study of 50 Chinese adults.[4] Psychological and biological aspects[5] and psychodynamic features[6] were compared between approaches in further cohort studies. Planning accuracy,[7] postoperative stability[8] and occlusal setup accuracy[9] have also been assessed.

Registered trials include a completed study of surgery-first in skeletal class III treatment (n=60, started 2022),[12] a study of surgery-first with aligners (recruiting, n=20),[13] and a retrospective study of a tooth-bone dual-support osteotomy locating plate in surgery-first treatment (n=20).[14] No large randomized trial results were identified in the sources reviewed.

card.summary: Jaw surgery done before (or without) braces; studied in cohorts, with treatment-time and stability findings that vary by study.
card.note: Major jaw surgery; general orthognathic risks apply, plus planning-specific precautions.

quick.overview:
Surgery-first reorders corrective jaw surgery: the bone operation comes before, or replaces, the long pre-surgical braces phase. Surgeons using it say better 3D planning and miniscrews make this possible.

Studies, mostly cohort comparisons in class III patients, have looked at treatment time, stability, quality of life and planning accuracy.
quick.mechanism: The jaw is repositioned according to a virtual plan with a pre-set surgical bite, and orthodontic tooth movement follows afterwards, often with miniscrew assistance.
quick.risks: Orthognathic surgery carries risks of bleeding, swelling, infection and nerve injury with numbness that is usually temporary. A 2019 review discusses precautions and complications specific to the surgery-first sequence.
